after: ## The four sectors and their features
alt: Four rows give the feature and examples of the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors. Below, a reminder to place the activity: in a mining company a geologist is primary but an office cashier is tertiary, and a delivery driver is tertiary.
caption: Ask what the worker actually does to place the activity in a sector.

alt: A grid of advantages and disadvantages of specialisation for an individual, a factory and a country, such as becoming skilled against boring work, higher output per worker against the whole line stopping, and export income against dependence on other countries.
caption: Each context has its own advantages and disadvantages; use the one the question names.

alt: Two panels. In-house production gives control on quality, control of information and fewer supplier delays. Outsourced production gives access to expertise, cost savings and lets managers focus on what the business does best.
caption: In-house means control; outsourcing means expertise and cost savings.

alt: A domestic supply chain has every stage in one country. A global one, such as a bicycle, has the frame welded in one country and the gears made in another, both sent to a third country for final assembly.
caption: A supply chain is global when at least some stages take place in other countries.

alt: Home trade runs producer, wholesaler, retailer, consumer. In international trade an agent finds buyers or sellers and arranges deals without holding the goods; a factor takes possession of the goods and sells them for the owner. Neither owns the goods; both earn commission.
caption: The factor holds the goods and the agent does not; neither owns them.

alt: Top: with EDI, a supermarket’s system sends an order to the supplier automatically when stock falls to a set level, and documents such as invoices come back electronically. Below, the gains and drawbacks of automation and of EDI.
caption: Both technologies speed up production and ordering but bring set-up costs and new risks.

after: ## Costs of trade, commerce and production
alt: A cost table for 500 exported jackets worth $20,000: transport 1,800, packaging 300, customs duties 1,000 (5%), agent’s commission 600 (3%), warehousing 300 and bank charges 45. Total $4,045, or $8.09 per jacket.
caption: Convert each percentage to dollars, add every line, then divide: $4,045 is $8.09 a jacket.
